messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: stan_scat within a for loop
parts:
Here's a tip for anyone using stan_scat. In attempting to run stan_scat on all pairs of parameters from a list of parameter, I ran into a bizarre and aggravating issue. Although

    stan_scat(fit, par_names[c(i,j)])

displays a posterior scatterplot of parameter par_names[i] versus par_names[j],

    for (i in 1:(n-1))
      for (j in (i+1):n)  {
        stan_scat(fit, par_names[c(i,j)])
        readline()
      }

displays absolutely nothing. Ditto for

    for (i in 1:1) stan_scat(fit, par_names[1:2])

This gave me considerable heartburn until I realized that stan_scat doesn't actually display anything -- it just returns a ggplot object, which you have to print() in order for it to be displayed. The command line automatically calls print() on the value of any expression entered, giving the illusion that stan_scat() itself is displaying the scatterplot when it is called in isolation.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: stan_scat within a for loop
parts:
Hi Kevin, 

You're right about the behavior, and it might indeed be bizarre, but it's not specific to rstan. It's how R and ggplot2 behave in general. For example:

library(ggplot2)

x <- rnorm(100)
qplot(x) # this will display a plot


for (j in 1:10) {
 x <- rnorm(100)
 qplot(x) # no plot displayed
 print(qplot(x)) # plot displayed
}


But this isn't only with ggplot2. For example: 

2 + 2 # the number 4 is printed


for (j in 1:10) {
 2 + 2 # nothing is printed
 print(2 + 2) # 4 is printed
}



For the rstan plotting functions that return a single ggplot object this is how they will behave. I suppose we could have them always call print internally, but then this would deviate from the typical behavior you get when using ggplot2. 

Jonah
